questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[-1,\text{ }1]^{T},$ respectively. Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Let's now sketch the phase portrait.

- First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274360/assets/18fad31b9f69e55d9f4bc414d3e1b732eaee7685bf36a183033fc302e911eb82.png)

- Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 
$y=-x$
and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274360/assets/f9d1127a2bdde6e2b9910a4404a73b9e8b994ff8400e8607af8b6931013f2533.png)

All other non-equilibrium solutions are parallel to the vector ${v}_{2}.$ So, the phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274360/assets/f4abb32b9a492e7d39b4504af7cf2a180e74dcca679804ed8198089cb68b7fb6.png)

questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $v=[2,\text{ }1]^{T}.$ The vector $w=[2,\text{ }0]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$  Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2t+2 \\ t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=\frac{1}{2}x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274360/assets/47deaca4362c32ef92833c1aae0c533a05314caf4ad4ccd2b685c3b4bc7436dc.png)

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2t+2 \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

For example:

- When ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2t+4 \\ y=t+1\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274360/assets/55741e66507ccc28af5bc5e7e347bf899c5c4bf2cc3d1a687be3c6c9c0fb4e01.png)

- When ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=-1,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2t-4 \\ y=-t-1\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274360/assets/1bc4e458b50d98fba82a3220d35982d5b034c0d64a5977bd2be81527b1b77f00.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274360/assets/5e822ce487f9ff6b4adbcf7a801a391b4ddf3f65d111a3c26f3a0c34fac8a45d.png)
